title: Purgatory (CCC 1030–1032)
hookLine: a purifying for those who die in God's friendship but not yet whole

cards: The invitation says seven. The host is someone you love. It's ten to seven; you've been gardening all day: dirt under your nails, sweat, a scratch on your arm.
You're welcome as you are; the invitation is real and isn't taken back. But at the door you might still say: give me a minute, let me wash first.
That wanting to be clean first is close to what the Church means by a word often heard as something darker.

teach.b: The Catechism says those who die in God's grace and friendship, but still imperfectly purified, are assured of their eternal salvation.
After death they undergo a purification, to gain the holiness needed to enter the joy of heaven. The Church calls it purgatory, from the Latin purgare: to cleanse.
It isn't a second chance for someone who refused God, or a smaller hell; the Catechism says it's entirely different from the punishment of the damned.

teach.h: ALREADY SAVED, ON THE WAY IN.
teach.b: Everyone there is already saved, on the way in. Catholics point to Paul: a person whose work burns up "shall be saved, yet so as by fire."
And to Second Maccabees, where Judas Maccabeus has an offering made for soldiers who had died: "It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from sins."

The Church, the Catechism says, has prayed for the dead from the beginning. Orthodox Christians pray for their dead too, without defining a purgatory in the same way; many Protestants don't hold the teaching.
One mix-up: purgatory isn't limbo. Limbo was a theory some theologians held about babies who die before baptism; the Church never made it a teaching.
The Catechism entrusts those children to God's mercy, with hope for their salvation. If that loss is yours, you don't have to carry it alone; in the US, 988 answers day and night.

teach.h: THE FIRE MAY BE HIS GAZE.
teach.b: Tradition speaks of a cleansing fire, and Benedict XVI suggested the fire might be Christ himself: meeting his gaze burns away what's false, and that pain is the pain of love, which heals.
On this view, purgatory isn't about being punished enough. It's about being loved until a person is whole.

how: Catholics pray for the dead at every Mass, have Masses offered for loved ones who have died, and keep All Souls Day on November 2, when many visit cemeteries to pray.

games.q: you're Judas Maccabeus. under the coats of some of your fallen soldiers are tokens taken from idols, which the law forbade. what do you do?
o: have an offering made for them, praying for the dead.
games.why: he sends an offering, and the text calls it a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead.

practice: Think of the dead nobody names: a worn stone in an old cemetery where the name has rubbed away, the person who lived in your home before you. No one may be thinking of them today.
If you pray, hold them in the old prayer for the dead or a few words of your own; if not, hold them in mind and wish them whole.

wordCard.voice: Purgatory. From the Latin for cleansing: the final purification, Catholics believe, of those who die in God's friendship but aren't yet whole. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: place or state of cleansing, from purgare, to cleanse.

carryVoice: Your line: purified by love. Not a smaller hell, but a washing before the dinner. Until tomorrow.
